1:
The writer names himself only by office, and Henry makes something of the reticence: the title belongs to him by years and by office alike, yet he almost levels himself with the ordinary pastors, since it does not become Christ's ministers to affect swelling pompous titles. He offers a second possibility, that the extraordinary ministers being now dead, this survivor took the commoner name to countenance the standing ministry that remained. Who the recipient was is the letter's first real dispute, and it runs five ways. Clarke sets out the candidates in order: the Caius who was Paul's host at Corinth, the Caius baptized there, probably the same man, the Macedonian who travelled with Paul, the Caius of Derbe known by his epithet, and this one, whom some separate from all the rest because the apostle ranks him among his own children. Gill argues the chronology, Paul's Caius living at Corinth and this one near Ephesus, with thirty or forty years between them; Ellicott says the difference in date alone settles it and adds that nothing shows whether the man was a presbyter. Wesley takes the other side, that he was probably the Corinthian, either removed into Asia or written to at Corinth. Henry declines to decide: if this is not he, it is his brother in name, estate and disposition. Barnes says only that nothing more is known of him.

Robertson counts the verbal adjective for "beloved" four times in these few lines, all of them of the same man, and Henry finds in the qualifying phrase either the sincerity of the affection or its religion: to love a friend for the truth's sake, as one abiding and walking in the truth, is gospel love, and love expressed is apt to kindle love. The prayer that follows has been mistranslated in a way Barnes takes some trouble to undo. The phrase rendered "above all things" means in respect of all things, not more than anything else; on the common rendering the apostle would be wishing his friend health and outward prosperity above his usefulness or his salvation, which cannot be the sense. What is meant is that in every respect it may go as well with him as it goes with his soul. Clarke divides the wish into three, health of body, health of soul and success in secular affairs, holds that every Christian may pray for all three, and adds that we should have more of them if we prayed for them devoutly; he notes too a manuscript that turns the second clause into a wish that Gaius be sound in the truth.

Robertson supplies the words themselves. The verb for prospering is built from the roots for a good journey, and the verb for health, which in Paul always means soundness of teaching, here means the body; he passes on a suggestion that Gaius's health may have been giving his friends anxiety, and calls the comparison remarkable, since it takes the welfare of the soul for granted before measuring anything against it. Gill keeps the first clause on worldly ground, success in the business of life, which depends on the blessing that maketh rich and is therefore a fit thing to pray for. Henry turns the standard round and gets an aphorism out of it: soul prosperity is the greatest blessing on this side of heaven, and grace and health are two rich companions, grace improving health and health employing grace. He grants that a rich soul is often lodged in a crazy body, where grace must be exercised in submitting to the dispensation, but holds it right to wish a healthy body for those whose souls prosper, their grace having then a larger sphere to shine in. Both he and Barnes end at the same uncomfortable place, observing that for most people the apostle's wish would have to be reversed before it could be prayed.
3:
Robertson insists the verb of rejoicing is not the epistolary aorist but a report of what the writer actually felt at the news, and reads the participles as marking repetition, brethren arriving from time to time and testifying each time they came. He passes on the observation that in these writings truth covers every sphere of life at once, moral, intellectual and spiritual, and notes that the pronoun is emphatic, this man being set against the one named later in the letter. Who the travellers were is guessed at rather than known. Gill takes them for preachers who went from place to place to spread the gospel, Clarke for the itinerant evangelists mentioned again a few verses on, and Barnes offers two possibilities: either members of the same church who had visited him for some reason, or the very brethren he had commended by letter, who were refused by the church and then entertained by Gaius, and who would naturally bear honourable testimony on their return. Henry attends instead to the fact that a report was made at all, remarking that a good report is owed by those who have received good, and that though a good name is a small enough reward for costly service, it is better than precious ointment.

He adds that the testimony was given before the church, and guesses at the motive, that out of the fulness of the heart the mouth spoke, or that the travellers wished to engage the congregation's prayers for the continued life and usefulness of such a patron. On the word for greater Robertson notes a curiosity, that it is a double comparative built on a comparative, the same formation that produces "lesser" in English and "more better" in the poets, and that forms like it turn up in the vernacular papyri, in Homer and in Shakespeare. He also records a manuscript that reads grace where the text has joy, and Gill arrives at the same variant from the Latin side, observing that the Vulgate reads grace or thanks and so makes the sense that the apostle had nothing to be more thankful for. Clarke glosses the truth found in Gaius as the soundness of his faith and the depth of his religion. Barnes hears the whole sentence as the language of an aged man speaking of converts who looked up to him as a father, and infers from it that Gaius was probably much the younger of the two.

The word "children" reopens the question of who this man was, and the four who take it up divide two against two. Barnes infers that Gaius had been converted under the apostle's own ministry, and Robertson allows that the noun may mean he was one of his converts. Clarke states the inference in order to resist it: it has been argued from this word that Gaius was John's convert and therefore not the Corinthian, but an old man had a right to address his juniors in age and grace as his children, and the word carries propriety and dignity coming from such a person. Wesley holds the same and puts the case more warmly, that Gaius was probably converted by Paul, so that the term is the tender style of paternal love whoever the instrument of conversion was, and that the appellation has a peculiar beauty from a writer calling himself the elder. On the joy itself there is no division. Wesley says such is the spirit of every true Christian pastor, and Barnes widens it from ministers to parents, holding that a child who wished to give his family the greatest possible happiness could do it in no other way, and that nothing gives more peace at a Christian's death than assurance on that point.
5:
The opening phrase is not quite settled. Robertson allows that it may mean either a faithful work or "thou makest sure," citing a parallel from Xenophon, and admits the point is not certain; Clarke reports a proposal that the adjective stands for the noun, so that the sense is keeping faith or keeping one's engagements, and glosses it as acting throughout as the Christian religion required. Wesley compresses it to uprightly and sincerely, and Gill adds the negative, that the giving was not done hypocritically to be seen of men and gain applause but from a principle of love. Barnes distinguishes the two classes benefited: brethren probably meaning Christians of his own congregation whom he knew, strangers meaning those who had arrived bearing a letter of commendation. Robertson draws a conclusion from the praise itself that reaches beyond this letter, observing that so warm a commendation of hospitality shows the refusal of hospitality urged in the second epistle to have been aimed at a particular case rather than laid down as a rule. Clarke, for his part, notes that nothing in the verse supports the penitential pilgrimages some have contrived to draw from it.

Sending the travellers forward is a technical courtesy rather than a vague kindness. Robertson traces the custom back to Homer, where the parting guest is sped on his way, sometimes by being accompanied and sometimes by being given money and food, notes that rabbis were escorted so, and adds that the polite formula translated "thou wilt do well" is the ordinary please of the letter-writing papyri. On the qualifying phrase he quotes the judgment that since these men are God's representatives they are to be treated as God would be. Barnes explains the aid as accompanying them, furnishing the means of the journey, or entertaining them, and raises a difficulty about the tense, the Greek pointing to a journey still to come while the letter seems to describe one already made; he resolves it by supposing a second visit in prospect. Clarke turns the verse on the reader and does not soften it, asking whether congregations who owe their preachers nothing by law deal with them in a way worthy of God, or leave them lacking the bread that perishes while they minister the bread of life without sparing; he notes that in the apostolic mission each church bore the cost of sending a man on to the next.

The name they went out for is left bare, and Robertson passes on the remark that it is in essence the whole Christian creed, the usage matching the absolute use of "the Way" in Acts. On their refusing support from the heathen he and Barnes agree as to motive, that the missionaries were guarding against the charge of being after money, which Robertson says his own century's missionaries still had to guard against, there having been in the ancient world many travelling lecturers out for pay. Clarke enters a caution against generalising it, since the maxim of the founder of the religion is that the labourer is worthy of his hire, and congregations that bear the whole expense of the gospel are the ones that prize it most. He then offers a construction nobody else considers: that the participle governs the following phrase, so that they were driven out by the Gentiles and went taking nothing, leaving their property behind in destitution, which he supports from a variant reading and from the verb's use elsewhere of being cast out. Gill has them driven out too, but by the unbelieving Jews of Judea. On the closing word Robertson notes that it may mean fellow workers with the brethren for the truth or fellow workers with the truth itself, and Barnes draws the practical inference, that those who cannot go may still contribute and so share the work.
9:
Whether a letter was actually sent is disputed, and the dispute turns on a particle. Clarke adopts the conditional rendering, that some manuscripts supply the word and judicious critics think it implied, so the sense is that the writer would have written to the church but knew his letter must pass through the hands of a man who would not acknowledge his authority, and therefore wrote to Gaius instead. Barnes sets out the same evidence, the Latin and Syriac versions and the later copies that introduce the particle, and rejects it on two grounds: the reading is not sustained by good authority, and the plain sense of the verb without the particle is that he wrote. Robertson calls the addition clearly spurious. Gill reports both versions without choosing. What the lost letter was is a second question. Barnes takes it for a note of commendation whose contents cannot now be recovered; Robertson agrees, denies that it was the second epistle, and objects to the argument that the indefinite pronoun proves the letter unimportant. Gill sees no difficulty in its not surviving, since not everything written to particular persons was kept, and observes that the first epistle cannot be meant, having nothing in it about relieving the brethren.

What office the man held is guessed at from the word describing his ambition, a verb so rare that Robertson finds it here and afterwards only in church writers. He cautions that loving the first place does not prove a bishop set over elders, an arrangement belonging to the next century; the man may have been an elder or a deacon and still have wanted to rule the whole congregation. Clarke thinks him an officer certainly, a deacon at least and probably a bishop, who magnified himself in the post; Wesley guesses the pastor. Henry draws the sting differently, observing that here is a minister less generous and communicative than the private Christians of the same church, and that ministers may sometimes be outshone and outdone; he adds that it ill becomes Christ's ministers to affect presidency in the church of God, and that ambition will breed malice against whoever opposes it. On the words used against the apostle, Robertson distinguishes idle chatter from malevolence and says the second is meant, remarking that the aged writer is not afraid of the man and openly defies him, and is the apostle of love for all that. Henry notes drily that to an aspiring spirit apostolic authority signifies little.

Clarke reduces the conduct to a proverb, that the man had the whole principle of the dog in the manger, neither doing nor letting do, and undoing whatever good was done that he did not approve; he guesses at a motive, that Diotrephes may have been a converted Jew unwilling to see Gentiles admitted, or a Judaizer who slandered the apostles for teaching otherwise. Robertson observes that the two verbs for hindering and casting out may each describe a single success, a repeated practice, or an attempt that failed, and declines to decide which. Barnes is careful about the threat that follows, insisting there is no evidence of a vindictive spirit, since a merely private affront might have been let drop, while what had happened was public and touched the apostle's authority, the church's duty and the character of the men commended. Henry states the principle underneath it, that a pastor is not at absolute liberty nor lord over God's heritage. The closing exhortation is read by everyone against this background. Gill takes the evil not to be imitated as the pride and preeminence and hardheartedness just described, and notes how far the example of men in authority carries, particularly in matters of charity, where following it saves money. Robertson observes that the writer stops short of saying whose the evildoer is, though he means it.
12:
Nothing certain is known of the man commended, and the guesses are recorded rather than settled. Gill offers the contraction of another name, the bearer of the letter from Ephesus, the Ephesian of that name in Acts, or a member of the same church. Robertson runs through the same list and rejects most of it, calling the identification with the deserter unlikely and saying of the silversmith only that one would like to believe he was converted under this ministry, though there is no evidence; he thinks the man may have carried the letter and fallen under suspicion, which would explain so warm a commendation. Barnes weighs one detail in favour of his belonging to the same congregation as Gaius, the phrase implying a testimony wider than the writer's own knowledge. On the witnesses themselves Robertson counts three, all men, the truth, and the writer with those about him, and raises the possibility that the second means the Holy Spirit rather than a personification, since the Spirit is elsewhere called the truth. Barnes takes it as the difference between a reputation resting on appearances and one resting on fact. Henry warns that few are well spoken of by all, that it is sometimes ill to be so, and that some have a good report but not of the truth itself.

The writing materials get more attention than one might expect. Robertson explains the two nouns as the black and the reed, and notes that a reed served for papyrus and parchment where a sharp stilus was used on wax; Clarke sets the pair against the previous letter, which named paper and ink where this one names ink and pen. Ellicott corrects the tense, that there were many things the writer had wished to write. On why they were withheld the readings differ in temper. Barnes suggests there may have been matters he would not wish exposed to the public eye, which fits a letter whose middle section names a man and describes his conduct. Henry keeps it practical, that many things are fitter for immediate speech than for a letter and that a little conversation spares the time, trouble and charge of much writing. The closing wish Ellicott takes to be deliberately chosen against the ordinary Greek farewell, which said be strong; this was instead the greeting given on the day of the resurrection, and he unfolds it in three, the inward peace of a good conscience, the outward peace of universal friendship, and the heavenly peace begun already in this life.

The last word of the letter is the one that interests them most. Ellicott calls the term for those saluted uncommon and hears in it the words of the upper room, where the disciples were told they were no longer servants; Wesley says the word for friend seldom occurs there at all, being swallowed up in the more endearing name of brother; Clarke reports that the older copies read brethren here, friends being a singular appellation found nowhere else in Scripture. On the instruction to greet them individually, Ellicott and Robertson arrive independently at the same passage, the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name, Robertson adding that the phrase occurs nowhere else in the New Testament though it is common in the letters preserved on papyrus. Ellicott observes that a long list of messages would be out of place in so short a private letter with a visit expected, and that Gaius would know the names as well as if written down. Clarke draws a conclusion from the whole ending that returns to where the letter began, taking the personal acquaintance it assumes as proof that this was not sent to Corinth, where the writer is unlikely ever to have been. Henry ends where the greeting does, that those may well salute one another on earth who hope to live together in heaven.
